quiz.q: How do you mark a function as a test that `cargo test` will run?
options: Put the word `test` in its name
Return a bool from the function
quiz.explain: The `#[test]` attribute is the sticker that tells Cargo to run this function during `cargo test`. Without it, the function is ignored by the test runner.

options: Prints a and b side by side
Fails (panics) the test if a is not equal to b
Returns true or false without stopping the test
quiz.explain: `assert_eq!` panics (marking the test failed) when the two values are not equal, and does nothing when they are. It's the workhorse assertion.

quiz.q: Why put `#[cfg(test)]` on your test module?
options: It makes the tests run faster
It compiles the test code only during `cargo test`, not into the real build
It is required or the tests won't be found
It turns off the borrow checker for tests
quiz.explain: `#[cfg(test)]` means the module is only compiled when testing, so your test-only code and imports never bloat the shipped program.

quiz.q: Where do integration tests live in a Cargo project?
options: They must be in the same function as the code
quiz.explain: Integration tests go in a top-level `tests/` folder; each file there is compiled as its own crate that uses your public API from the outside, like a real user.

flashcards.front: How do you run all tests in a Cargo project?
flashcards.back: `cargo test` — it finds every `#[test]` function, runs them, and reports pass/fail.
Unit tests live next to the code (in a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` block) and can see private items. Integration tests live in the `tests/` folder and only see the public API.

flashcards.front: What happens to a `#[test]` function with no assertions?
flashcards.back: It always passes — it's checking nothing. Every test needs at least one assert to be meaningful.
Marks a test that passes only if the code inside panics — used when panicking is the correct behavior.
